title: Meet the Image Before You Make It Yours
subtitle: A half-hour with a cultural image can reveal more than what is pictured. Try this two-person exercise to look closely, check the record and make a more considered choice about sharing or reuse.
imageAlt: Two friends sit at a kitchen table with a laptop open to a museum collection record, a notebook between them and a printed archival photograph nearby.
imageConcept: Two friends at a sunlit kitchen table compare a printed archival photograph with its collection record on a laptop, taking notes before deciding whether to share or adapt it.
body: Start with the record, not the download button

A compelling image can seem to arrive on its own: a portrait, a pattern, a scene from another time. But an image in a cultural collection comes with a trail of information—often a title, creator, date, collection, description and rights statement. Spending time with that trail changes the task. Instead of asking only, “Can I use this?” you can also ask, “What do I know about what I’m seeing, and what remains unknown?”

That distinction matters because permission and context answer different questions. A record that marks an image as reusable can help establish whether a particular use is allowed under the stated terms. It does not necessarily tell you how the people pictured would feel about the image being circulated, whether a caption is complete, or what the image meant in its original setting. Looking carefully is not a substitute for rights research; rights research is not a substitute for looking carefully.
Choose an image whose reuse status is explicit

For this exercise, pick one image from a cultural institution’s collection whose own item record clearly indicates that it is available for your proposed reuse. Smithsonian Open Access is one place to explore: at its 2020 launch, the Smithsonian announced that 2.8 million 2D and 3D images and 173 years of staff-created data were released into the public domain as CC0 [1]. That is a launch-era description, not a current collection total, and it should not be read as saying every item in every collection is available on the same terms.

Open the individual item record and read its rights information rather than relying on a search result, a repost, or a general impression that a museum’s collection is open. The Smithsonian’s launch announcement said covered material could be downloaded, transformed and shared without permission from the institution [3]. The key word is covered: check the record for the particular image and make sure its stated status fits what you want to do. If the terms are unclear, choose another image rather than treating uncertainty as permission.
Give the image and the record equal attention

Set aside about half an hour and invite a friend to join you. Choose a comfortable place where you can both see the image and its record. Before reading the description, spend a few minutes noticing the image itself. Each person can write down three details: one thing that draws the eye, one relationship or gesture you notice, and one question you have. Keep these observations specific. “The figure’s hand is near the edge of the frame” is more useful than “It feels old.”

Now read the record together. Note the title, creator if listed, date or estimated date, collection name, description and rights statement. Follow the collection link if it offers more context. Some records are detailed; others are sparse. Don’t fill a gap with a confident guess. If the creator is unknown, say that the record does not name one. If a date is approximate, keep it approximate. The image and its catalog description are both sources of information, but neither guarantees that every relevant detail is present.
Separate permission from the questions that remain

The Library of Congress advises users to consult an item’s “Rights and Access” information for possible restrictions or permissions. It also cautions that being unable to locate a rights holder does not, by itself, make a work free to use, and asks researchers to approach collection materials with respect for the culture and sensibilities of the people represented [2]. Those cautions point to two different kinds of care: establish the rights status, and consider what your use might communicate or expose.

For each image, ask what the record establishes and what it does not. Does it identify the person, place or event—or simply describe visible features? Does it explain how the image entered the collection? Is there a cultural or historical context that would affect how you present it? Could your crop, caption or design suggest something the record does not support? These are not reasons to assume an image is off limits; they are prompts to be precise and thoughtful.

In the United States, copyright is not determined by age alone in every case, and exceptions such as fair use depend on circumstances. A reuse label is useful evidence about the stated rights, but it is not a universal answer to privacy, publicity or other concerns. When a project carries legal, commercial or personal stakes, consult the institution’s guidance or a qualified professional. This exercise is an invitation to look more carefully, not legal advice.
Write two short notes before deciding

Each person now writes two brief responses, then reads them aloud if comfortable. First: “This image invites me to notice…” Name a concrete detail or relationship rather than making a claim about the people pictured. Second: “The record does not establish…” This might be a person’s identity, the purpose of an object, the circumstances of a photograph, or simply something the catalog does not explain. You can also write that the record does not answer a question you had.

Compare notes without trying to reach one shared interpretation. You may notice different things; that difference is useful. One person might focus on a subject’s expression while the other notices the framing or the surrounding objects. Ask what in the image or record led each of you there. If you disagree, keep the disagreement visible rather than treating one reading as the definitive story. The point is not to solve the image. It is to distinguish observation from inference and to make room for uncertainty.
If you share or adapt it, carry the context along

Before posting, printing or transforming the image, return to the item record. Preserve the title, creator as listed, collection link and rights information alongside the image. If you crop, recolor, add text or place it in a new setting, make clear that it has been adapted when that distinction matters. Don’t let a new caption imply facts the record does not support, and don’t present your interpretation as the institution’s description.

Consider the destination, too. A classroom handout, a private note and a public campaign put an image before different audiences and give it different force. Ask whether your use changes the image’s meaning, makes a person or community the object of a joke, or strips away context that would help viewers understand it. The answers may lead you to share it, adapt it with a careful caption, keep it for study, or choose another image. All are legitimate outcomes. Permission makes a use possible under stated terms; it does not obligate you to use the image.

Close by looking once more at the image and the record together. Each person names one thing they understand more clearly now and one question that remains. Save the item link with your notes, so the source and its rights information stay attached if you return to the image later. If you decide to use it, keep those details with the copy you share. If you decide not to, you have still done something worthwhile: you have practiced seeing a cultural image not as raw material waiting to be claimed, but as an object with a creator, a record, limits and a life beyond your own response.

Try the exercise with one image, not a whole collection. Half an hour is enough to discover that looking closely does not always produce certainty. Sometimes it produces a more honest caption, a more careful choice—or the recognition that the record leaves room for questions worth carrying forward.
